title: Babylonian astronomy and mathematics
summary: Babylonian civilization replaced that of the Sumerians from around 2000 BCE, and built on their sexagesimal, or base 60, counting. Babylonian mathematicians solved quadratic equations and divided the day into 24 hours, each hour into 60 minutes and each minute into 60 seconds, a count that has survived for 4,000 years. By the 17th century BCE, their astronomy had well defined the year and other cycles of time.

uncertainty.note: St Andrews traces Babylonian mathematics replacing Sumerian from around 2000 BC; World History Encyclopedia dates Babylonian prominence from circa 1792 to circa 600 BCE and notes development of astronomical cycles by the 17th century BCE.

where.historical_name: Babylon, Mesopotamia (capital of the Old Babylonian Kingdom and center of cuneiform scribal scholarship)

importance.justification: Babylonian base-60 positional mathematics, quadratic algebra, and systematic celestial observation established the foundations of world timekeeping, trigonometry, and classical astronomical calculation.
